The golden mouse (Ochrotomys nuttalli) is a small, semi-arboreal cricetid rodent endemic to the southeastern United States, where it inhabits dense thickets and forested wetlands. Neonates are altricial, weighing approximately 2.7 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.7 grams] at parturition, a modest initial mass that reflects the species' strategy of producing multiple, relatively small litters rather than investing heavily in a single offspring. This low neonatal mass relative to the ultimate adult body size—females typically attain a maximum body mass of 22 grams [Wwi = 22 grams]—places the species among the smaller-bodied rodents in its community, where it competes with but is often subordinate to the more aggressive Peromyscus species. The interplay between birth mass and eventual adult size underscores a life history that prioritizes rapid population turnover, a pattern that becomes evident when examining the species' reproductive schedule under thermoneutral conditions.

Reproduction in the golden mouse is tightly constrained by thermal physiology, with most key developmental milestones measured at a core body temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. Gestation is relatively short, lasting approximately 30 days [tg = approximately 30 days] at this temperature, a duration common among small murid rodents and one that facilitates multiple litters within a single b at a temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]reeding season. The weaning period begins approximately 21 days after birth [tx = approximately 21 days after birth] at 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C], though field observations suggest that complete nutritional independence may be delayed until 28 to 30 days, depending on maternal condition and resource availability. This relatively early weaning age allows females to rapidly return to reproductive condition, contributing to the species' high annual fecundity. The tight coupling of gestation length and weaning timing with thermal homeostasis highlights how even minor deviations from thermoneutrality can alter the pace of the reproductive cycle in this small endotherm.

Puberty in the golden mouse is achieved at 61 days after birth [tp = 61 days after birth] under the typical thermoneutral condition of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C], a developmental interval that is moderate among North American cricetids. This relatively early attainment of sexual maturity enables individuals born early in the spring to contribute to the breeding population before the summer solstice, thereby maximizing the number of reproductive windows available within a single season. The synchronization of pubertal development with thermal stability is biologically significant, as the energetic demands of gonadal maturation are substantial for a species with an ultimate wet weight of just 22 grams [Wwi = 22 grams]. Field studies have demonstrated that juveniles born later in the summer may delay the onset of puberty, effectively overwintering as sub-adults and initiating reproductive activity the following spring. Such plasticity in maturation timing buffers the population against the stochastic effects of late-season resource shortages and helps maintain overall reproductive output across variable years.

The maximum reproductive output of the golden mouse is among the highest recorded for small southeastern rodents. Females can produce up to 10 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 10 litters per year], with each litter containing an average of 2.7 pups [N_R_i = each litter containing an average of 2.7 pups] under favorable conditions. This yields a prodigious annual reproductive capacity that allows populations to recover rapidly from perturbations such as controlled burns or severe droughts. The combination of a short gestation period, early weaning, and rapid post-weaning maturation underpins this high fecundity; indeed, most of the life cycle unfolds at the species' characteristic body temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. In the context of life-history theory, Ochrotomys nuttalli exemplifies a fast-paced strategy, diverting a large proportion of acquired energy into reproduction at the expense of prolonged somatic investment. This strategy is viable in the relatively mild and productive environment of the southeastern United States, where long breeding seasons and abundant soft-mast crops provide the nutritional foundation for sustained high reproductive effort.

Despite its high fecundity, the golden mouse exhibits a comparatively modest maximum lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals living approximately 3,066 days [am = approximately 3,066 days] when maintained at a body temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. This longevity estimate, equivalent to roughly 8.4 years, places it near the upper bound for small-bodied cricetids and suggests that the species faces relatively low extrinsic mortality in its preferred dense-thicket habitat. The combination of an annual reproductive rate of 27 pups per female per year—derived from multiple annual litters and litter sizes—with a lifespan of more than eight years creates the potential for substantial lifetime reproductive output. This demographic profile, characterized by early maturation, high fecundity, and moderate longevity, is consistent with a species that experiences seasonal but not catastrophic mortality pressures. The ability to sustain reproductive activity over multiple years, even at a reduced rate in older females, likely buffers local populations against the periodic failures of particular mast crops. Future work should focus on quantifying age-specific fecundity and the physiological costs of sustained high reproductive output in this species.
